Cryptography & the Occult 6 texts, 12 editions

Cryptographic, hermetic, demonological, and angelological works. Includes the Polygraphia treatises, the Clavis works, the Sigilla, and the Liber Octo Quaestionum (responses to Maximilian on witchcraft).

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem

A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian · 1515first English

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's reply to the eight questions Maximilian put to him at Boppard: on faith and understanding, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles of unbelievers, on witches and harmful magic, and on related matters. Composed in 1508, it is his central statement on witchcraft and the source from which later demonological writers drew heavily. The questions are set out in an enumerated table and answered in sequence, in the blend of scholastic authority and pastoral caution that marks his shorter treatises.

4 editions: Oppenheym, 1515 · Coloniae, 1534 · Francoforti, 1550 · Moguntiae, 1601

Clavis Polygraphiae

Key to the Polygraphia · 1518

Clavis Polygraphiae — the "Key to the Polygraphia" — is Trithemius's own commentary on his Polygraphiae libri sex, explaining how the six books of cipher tables are constructed and how a correspondent is meant to use them in practice. A cipher manual is of little use without its key, and the Clavis is what made the Polygraphiae operational: it walks through the modi of enciphering and deciphering, the Ave Maria alphabets, and the polyalphabetic tables, tying the abstract apparatus of the six books to the concrete business of sending and recovering a hidden message. It was composed alongside the Polygraphiae in 1508 and printed with it.

Basel, 1518 · Latin / English

Polygraphiae libri VI (Basel: Furter & Petri, for Haselberg, 1518)

Six Books of Polygraphy (Basel, 1518 first edition) · 1518

Polygraphiae libri VI — "Six Books of Polygraphy" — is the 1518 first edition of Trithemius's open cryptographic manual, the first printed book on cryptography in the West. He completed the work late in life — the dedication to Emperor Maximilian I is dated 1508 — and it was printed posthumously, two years after his death. Where the Steganographia hides its ciphers behind angel-magic, the Polygraphiae teaches the craft in the open: substitution tables, transposition grids, the "Ave Maria" cipher in which any plaintext becomes a pious Latin sentence, and numerical codes. Its six books move from simple to complex, culminating in the polyalphabetic tabula recta.

3 editions: Basel, 1518 · Francofurti, 1550 · Argentoratum, 1600

Clavis Generalis Triplex in Libros Steganographicos

Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books · 1608

Clavis Generalis Triplex in Libros Steganographicos — the "Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books" — is Trithemius's own explanatory key to his most notorious work, the Steganographia. The Steganographia (composed around 1499–1500) circulated only in manuscript during his lifetime and earned him lasting accusations of necromancy, because its cipher instructions are dressed as conjurations of angels and spirits; it was printed posthumously in 1606 and placed on the Index. The Clavis is the antidote Trithemius supplied: a compact decryption key demonstrating that the "spirit names" resolve into a cryptographic system, not a magical one. It sets out, modus by modus, the explicit substitution alphabets by which each cipher is to be read.

Francofurti, 1608 · Latin / English

Veterum Sophorum Sigilla et Imagines Magicae (pseudo-Trithemian, 1612)

Seals and Magical Images of the Ancient Sages (pseudo-Trithemian astral-magic text) · 1612first English

Veterum Sophorum Sigilla et Imagines Magicae — "The Seals and Magical Images of the Ancient Sages" — is a short astral-magical text: instructions for engraving planetary seals and images on stones and gems, keyed to the divine name Tetragrammaton and the courses of the planets, "for producing miraculous effects." It belongs to the later esoteric corpus that attached itself to Trithemius's name after his death.

2 editions: Marne / Aubry, 1612 · e-rara, 1612

Steganographia, hoc est: Ars per occultam scripturam

Steganography: The Art of Hidden Writing · 1621

The Steganographia is Trithemius's most famous and most notorious work: a treatise in three books, written about 1499–1500 and circulated for a century in manuscript before it was first printed (Frankfurt, 1606). On its surface it is a manual of angel-magic — long conjurations addressed to spirit-princes and their subordinate spirits, each governing a quarter of the heavens, a wind, or an hour of the day. Beneath that surface it is a cryptographic system: the "conjurations" are cover-text, and the real message is carried by the spirit-names and the numeric keys tabulated for each prince. It was the disguise that undid him. Manuscript copies reached readers they were not meant for — Carolus Bovillus among them — who took the spirit-magic at face value and accused Trithemius of necromancy; the book was placed on the Index, and the third book's reputation as genuinely demonic persisted until its cipher was solved — first by Thomas Ernst (1996), then independently by Jim Reeds (1998). Trithemius's own answer to the charge is the Trithemius sui ipsius vindex of 1616, also in this corpus (prdl-32287).

Darmbstadii. Ex officina typographica Balthasaris Aulæandri, 1621 · Latin / English

Monastic Reform 8 texts, 12 editions

Works on monastic observance, the state of the orders, claustral life, exhortations to monks, and chapter resolutions. Includes De Laude Scriptorum Manualium (manuscript culture is a monastic register).

Abbreviatura Recessuum Capitularium Patrum Ordinis Divi Benedicti per Provinciam Moguntinam et Dioecesim Bambergensem

An Abridgment of the Chapter Decrees of the Fathers of the Order of St Benedict for the Province of Mainz and the Diocese of Bamberg · 1493first English

Abbreviatura Recessuum Capitularium Patrum Ordinis Divi Benedicti — "An Abridgment of the Chapter Decrees of the Fathers of the Order of St Benedict, for the Province of Mainz and the Diocese of Bamberg" — is Trithemius's digest of the recessus, the closing decrees of the Benedictine reform chapters. It is a working document of the Bursfelde-aligned observant reform rather than a treatise: a codified summary of the chapters' rulings on monastic discipline, the sort of administrative-legislative text an abbot kept to hand. As such it is the documentary counterpart to his reform polemics — the De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and the Sermones ad Monachos — showing the machinery behind the rhetoric.

Nürnberg, 1493 · Latin / English

De Republica Ecclesiae et Monachorum Ordinis

On the Commonwealth of the Church and the Order of Monks · 1493first English

De Republica Ecclesiae et Monachorum Ordinis — "On the Commonwealth of the Church and the Order of Monks" — is one of Trithemius's monastic-reform tracts, treating the right ordering of the religious life within the wider body of the Church. It belongs to the cluster of reform writings he produced as abbot of Sponheim in the 1490s — alongside De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — pressing for the restoration of strict Benedictine observance against the lax monasticism of his day. Its scope is wider than the purely cloistral: it sets the monastery within the commonwealth of the Church and the duties of the religious life within it.

2 editions: Mainz, 1493 · Mainz, 1493

De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis

On the State and Ruin of the Monastic Order · 1493first English

De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis — "On the State and Ruin of the Monastic Order" — is Trithemius's diagnostic of what had gone wrong with fifteenth-century Benedictine life. He wrote it as abbot of Sponheim in the mid-1490s, at the height of his reform programme: a generation after the Bursfelde Congregation had begun reorganising German monasticism around strict observance, he surveys the decay — property-holding, absenteeism, the collapse of the common life — and prescribes the return to the Rule. It is the sharpest of his reform tracts, and the one in which his disappointment is least concealed; it cost him goodwill among the abbots he had hoped to lead.

Leipzig, 1493 · Latin / English

De Laude Scriptorum Manualium

In Praise of Scribes · 1494

De Laude Scriptorum Manualium — "In Praise of Scribes" — is Trithemius's short tractatus defending the monastic labour of hand-copying manuscripts at the very moment the printing press was making it obsolete. He composed it in 1492, as abbot of Sponheim, and addressed it to Gerlach, abbot of Deutz. The argument turns on the spiritual discipline of the scribe — the patient, prayerful labour of the copyist as a form of contemplation and a defence against the devil — rather than on any hostility to print as such (Trithemius had his own works printed, and was an enthusiastic patron of the new art). It is one of the most charming and most-quoted of his shorter writings.

Mainz, 1494 · Latin / English

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum

On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks · 1498first English

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum — "On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks" — is Trithemius's ascetic guide to the monastic life, mapping the monk's progress through three "regions" or stages of interior discipline: purification for beginners, illumination for the proficient, and union with God for the perfect — a scheme drawn from Pseudo-Dionysius and the Victorines and adapted to Benedictine observance. He completed it in manuscript in 1497; it is one of the central texts of his Sponheim reform programme, alongside the Sermones ad Monachos and De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis.

3 editions: nobili vrbe Maguntina, 1498 · Mainz, 1498 · Lipsia, 1516

Compendium sive Breviarium primi voluminis Annalium sive Historiarum de origine regum et gentis Francorum

A Compendium or Breviary of the First Volume of the Annals or Histories, on the Origin of the Kings and People of the Franks · 1515first English

Compendium sive Breviarium primi voluminis Annalium sive Historiarum de origine regum et gentis Francorum — "A Compendium of the First Volume of the Annals on the Origin of the Kings and People of the Franks" — is Trithemius's condensed history of Frankish origins, dedicated to Lorenz von Bibra, Bishop of Würzburg. It is an abridgment of the larger annalistic project of his Würzburg years, and it shares the legendary-genealogical method characteristic of his historiography: a Trojan / Sicambrian descent for the Franks that later scholarship has treated with considerable caution. The compendium form makes it the most readable entry point into his Frankish history, set out year by year from the origins to the Carolingians.

Mainz, 1515 · Latin / English

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos

Sermons and Exhortations to Monks · 1516first English

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Sermons and Exhortations to Monks" — collects Trithemius's addresses to the monastic community at Sponheim during his reforming abbacy (1483–1506). The sermons are practical spiritual direction for Benedictine monks: on obedience, humility, the discipline of the choir, the dangers of private property, and the interior life that the Rule is meant to form. They sit at the heart of the monastic-reform cluster, alongside De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — less a systematic treatise than the abbot's own voice, pressing his monks toward the observance he wanted for them.

2 editions: Argentine, 1516 · Argentine, 1516

Admonitiones / Exhortationes ad Monachos

Admonitions and Exhortations to Monks (later collected reprint) · original date uncertainfirst English

Admonitiones / Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Admonitions and Exhortations to Monks" — gathers Trithemius's monastic-reform addresses: calls to stricter observance of the Benedictine Rule, to the interior life of the cloister, and to the duties of the professed monk. They belong to the reforming side of his abbacy — of a piece with the Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — and they show the abbot as pastor rather than polymath, urging his monks toward the discipline that his historical and cryptographic works were sometimes thought to have distracted him from.

Romae, 1898 · Latin / English

Marian & Hagiographic 3 texts, 9 editions

Marian devotion (especially the Anne / immaculate-conception tradition), Carmelite hagiography.

De Laudibus Sanctissimae Matris Annae

In Praise of the Most Holy Mother Anne · 1494first English

De Laudibus Sanctissimae Matris Annae — "In Praise of the Most Holy Mother Anne" — is Trithemius's treatise honouring St Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary and a focus of intense late-medieval devotion. He wrote it at Sponheim with a dedicatory letter to Rumold Laupach dated 1 July 1494, and it appeared with a cluster of commendatory poems on the Holy Kindred — the extended family of Christ that Anne, thrice-married in the apocryphal tradition, was held to have matriarched. It is a characteristic piece of his early Sponheim Marian-hagiographic output, leaning on the legendary material the Reformation would soon sweep away.

6 editions: Mainz, 1494 · Mainz, 1494 · Leipzig [ca. 1497, 1497 · Liptzk [ca. 1497, 1497 · Liptzk [ca. 1501, 1501 · Liptzk, 1501

De Origine, Progressu et Laudibus Ordinis Fratrum Carmelitarum

On the Origin, Progress, and Praises of the Order of Carmelite Brothers · 1494first English

De Origine, Progressu et Laudibus Ordinis Fratrum Carmelitarum — "On the Origin, Progress, and Praises of the Order of Carmelite Brothers" — is Trithemius's defence of the Carmelite order, written in 1492. It rehearses the order's claimed descent from the prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel — a foundation legend the mendicant orders pressed hard in the fifteenth century against humanist and conciliar scepticism — and catalogues its worthies in the bio-bibliographical manner Trithemius would soon make his own in the De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis. It belongs to the hagiographic-defensive side of his early output, and shows the historian of orders already at work a decade before the great chronicles.

Mainz [not before 1494, 1494 · Latin / English

De Purissima et Immaculata Conceptione Virginis (Buda)

On the Most Pure and Immaculate Conception of the Virgin (Buda edition) · 1497first English

De Purissima et Immaculata Conceptione Virginis — "On the Most Pure and Immaculate Conception of the Virgin" — is Trithemius's defence of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary, then a contested theological question rather than defined dogma, with Dominicans and Franciscans sharply divided. Trithemius argues for the Franciscan, pro-Immaculist side in the scholastic manner, and the work is continuous with his St Anne and Marian writings — the devotional-hagiographic strand of his early Sponheim output carried into doctrinal polemic.

2 editions: Nürnberg, 1497 · Argentoratum, 1506

Bibliography & History 4 texts, 5 editions

Catalog and biographical works — De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis and the Spanheim/Würzburg collected-works compilations and chronicles.

Liber de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis

On Ecclesiastical Writers · 1494first English

Liber de Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis — "On Ecclesiastical Writers" — is Trithemius's pioneering bio-bibliography of Christian authors, from the apostolic age to his own century, in roughly a thousand numbered entries: each author given a short biography and a list of writings. Completed at Sponheim in 1494 and printed at Basel by Johann Amerbach in the same year, it continues the catalogue tradition of Jerome, Gennadius, and Isidore on a far larger scale, and it stands as a founding text in the history of bibliography — the first large-scale alphabetical bio-bibliography of Christian literature, and the work for which Trithemius was best known in his lifetime.

2 editions: Basel, 1494 · Coloniae, 1546

De Septem Secundeis, id est, Intelligentiis sive Spiritibus Orbes post Deum Moventibus

On the Seven Secondary Intelligences, that is, the Spirits Moving the Orbs after God · 1522

De Septem Secundeis, id est, Intelligentiis sive Spiritibus Orbes post Deum Moventibus — "On the Seven Secondary Intelligences, that is, the Spirits Moving the Orbs after God" — is Trithemius's astrological philosophy of history. Its thesis is that the successive ages of the world are governed in turn by seven planetary angels — the secundeis — each ruling for a fixed period in the order of the celestial spheres, yielding a chronological scheme that runs from the Creation down to his own century. Addressed to Emperor Maximilian I, it is the work in which Trithemius brought his reading of the celestial-intelligence tradition (transmitted through Arabic and scholastic astronomy) to bear on universal history, and it had an outsized afterlife in Renaissance historical thought.

Nurnberge, 1522 · Latin / English

Opera Historica, Part I

Collected Historical Works (Freher ed.), first part · 1601first English

Opera Historica — "Historical Works," Part I — is the collected historical magnum opus of Trithemius's last years, assembling his chronicle of the Franks from their mythical Trojan origins through the Merovingian and Carolingian dynasties to the late medieval period. It follows the universal-chronicle tradition — year-by-year entries assembled from over two hundred manuscript sources — and is an important, if at times credulous, source for early medieval history. (Part II, the Hirsau and Sponheim monastic chronicles, is prdl-70290 in this corpus.) Like much of Trithemius's historical writing it mingles genuine documentary labour with fabricated sources, the most notorious being the invented Hunibald; readers should weigh it against later scholarship, but the breadth of compilation is real.

Francofurti, 1601 · Latin / English

Opera Historica, Part II — Chronicon Hirsaugiense & Sponheimense

Collected Historical Works, second part: the Hirsau and Sponheim chronicles · 1601first English

Opera Historica, Part II — the Chronicon Hirsaugiense and Chronicon Sponheimense — is the second half of Trithemius's collected historical works: his two great monastic chronicles. The Chronicon Hirsaugiense narrates the foundation and progress of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, down to 1520; the Chronicon Sponheimense does the same for his own former house of Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz. Together they are the fullest record of the Benedictine reform world he inhabited — though, like his Frankish history, they must be read with caution for the fabricated sources woven into the genuine documentary labour.

Francofurti, 1601 · Latin / English

The Priestly Life 3 texts, 4 editions

Pastoral and priestly works — pastoral care, the formation of priests, the priestly vocation.

Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis (Mainz, 1499)

On the Institution of the Priestly Life (Mainz, 1499) · 1494first English

Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis — "The Formation of the Priestly Life" — is Trithemius's treatise on the discipline, study, and conduct proper to priests. It is part of the clerical-formation strand of his work — alongside De Cura Pastorali and De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda — that runs parallel to the Benedictine reform writings. Its concern is the secular and regular clergy's interior and moral preparation rather than monastic observance as such: how a priest is to live, read, pray, and conduct himself in office.

2 editions: Mainz, 1494 · Augsburg, 1494

De Cura Pastorali

On Pastoral Care · 1496first English

De Cura Pastorali — "On Pastoral Care" — is Trithemius's treatise on the duties of those charged with the care of souls, in the long tradition of clerical-formation literature descending from Gregory the Great's Regula Pastoralis. It sits among his writings on the priestly and clerical life — alongside Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis and De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda — rather than his strictly monastic-reform tracts, though the two strands overlap in his work. Its concern is the rector's responsibility for those under his cure: preaching, correction, the example of life, and the burden of office.

Mainz [not before 1496, 1496 · Latin / English

De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda Libellus

A Little Book on Establishing the Life of Priests · 1577first English

De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda Libellus — "A Little Book on Establishing the Life of Priests" — is Trithemius's short treatise on ordering the life and conduct of priests, close in subject to his Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis and De Cura Pastorali. It belongs to the clerical-formation side of his work rather than the strictly monastic reform tracts: the "little book" of the title signals a compact, practical manual — how a priest is to be formed in virtue and learning — rather than a sustained treatise.

Devotional 3 texts, 3 editions

Contemplative and ascetic works — divine love, the vanity of human life, conversion of the mind to God.

De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae

On the Vanity and Misery of Human Life · 1495first English

De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae — "On the Vanity and Misery of Human Life" — is Trithemius's contribution to the contemptus mundi tradition, the medieval meditation on the transience and wretchedness of earthly existence descending from Innocent III's De Miseria Humanae Conditionis. It belongs to the devotional-contemplative strand of his output, alongside De Operatione Divini Amoris and De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum, and it rehearses the familiar themes — death, judgement, the emptiness of honours and riches — in the sober monastic register of his shorter treatises.

Mainz, 1495 · Latin / English

De Operatione Divini Amoris

On the Working of Divine Love · 1497first English

De Operatione Divini Amoris — "On the Working of Divine Love" — is one of Trithemius's devotional-contemplative works, treating the action of divine love in the soul. It belongs with the inward, affective side of his output rather than the polemical reform tracts or the cryptographic books, and stands near his other contemplative pieces in the corpus — De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum and De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae. Where the reform writings address the discipline of the cloister, this one turns to the inner motion of charity that the discipline is meant to serve.

Mainz, 1497 · Latin / English

De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum

On the True Conversion of the Mind to God · 1500first English

De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum — "On the True Conversion of the Mind to God" — is one of Trithemius's devotional-contemplative treatises, on the soul's genuine turning toward God as opposed to a merely outward religious life. It sits with the inward, affective side of his work — De Operatione Divini Amoris, De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae — rather than the reform tracts or the cryptographic books, and it treats conversion as an interior act of the will and intellect rather than a change of habit or observance.

Mainz, 1500 · Latin / English

Apologetic 1 text, 1 edition

Self-defense / apologetic works (one work: Sui Ipsius Vindex).

Trithemius Sui Ipsius Vindex

Trithemius, Vindicator of Himself · 1616first English

Trithemius Sui Ipsius Vindex — "Trithemius, Vindicator of Himself" — is the abbot's apologetic answer to the accusations of demonic magic that dogged his last decade. His Steganographia, circulated in manuscript from the late 1490s and reaching readers it was not meant to reach — Carolus Bovillus among them — had been read at face value as a manual of necromancy, and the charge clung to him; the Vindex, printed posthumously in 1616, gathers his own protestations of orthodoxy alongside the testimony of allies, insisting that the Steganographia is cryptography dressed as conjuration, not magic at all. It is the apologetic counterpart to the Steganographia (prdl-24395) and the Clavis Generalis Triplex (prdl-70281) elsewhere in this corpus.

Ingolstadii, 1616 · Latin / English

Verse 1 text, 1 edition

Occasional Latin verse (one work: the bald-men ecloga to Maximilian).

Ecloga de Laude Calvorum ad Carolum (Hucbald of Elnon, transmitted by Trithemius)

An Eclogue in Praise of Bald Men, to Charles (Hucbald of Elnon; in Trithemius’s transcription) · 1496first English

The Ecloga de Laude Calvorum ad Carolum — "An Eclogue in Praise of Bald Men, to Charles" — is one of the legendary curiosities of medieval Latin literature: a 133-line poem in which every single word begins with the letter C. It is a lipogrammatic tour de force, an entire mock-encomium conducted under that one constraint — the bald-headed are like the sun, like the moon, like polished bronze, like a clear and unclouded sky — and the constraint is the joke as much as the praise. Composed in the Carolingian ninth century and addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald, it earned its author a small immortality outside his more serious musical and hagiographic writings.

Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis (Mainz, 1499)

On the Institution of the Priestly Life (Mainz, 1499) · 1494first English

Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis — "The Formation of the Priestly Life" — is Trithemius's treatise on the discipline, study, and conduct proper to priests. It is part of the clerical-formation strand of his work — alongside De Cura Pastorali and De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda — that runs parallel to the Benedictine reform writings. Its concern is the secular and regular clergy's interior and moral preparation rather than monastic observance as such: how a priest is to live, read, pray, and conduct himself in office.

2 editions: Mainz, 1494 · Augsburg, 1494

De Origine, Progressu et Laudibus Ordinis Fratrum Carmelitarum

On the Origin, Progress, and Praises of the Order of Carmelite Brothers · 1494first English

De Origine, Progressu et Laudibus Ordinis Fratrum Carmelitarum — "On the Origin, Progress, and Praises of the Order of Carmelite Brothers" — is Trithemius's defence of the Carmelite order, written in 1492. It rehearses the order's claimed descent from the prophet Elijah on Mount Carmel — a foundation legend the mendicant orders pressed hard in the fifteenth century against humanist and conciliar scepticism — and catalogues its worthies in the bio-bibliographical manner Trithemius would soon make his own in the De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis. It belongs to the hagiographic-defensive side of his early output, and shows the historian of orders already at work a decade before the great chronicles.

Mainz [not before 1494, 1494 · Latin / English

De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae

On the Vanity and Misery of Human Life · 1495first English

De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae — "On the Vanity and Misery of Human Life" — is Trithemius's contribution to the contemptus mundi tradition, the medieval meditation on the transience and wretchedness of earthly existence descending from Innocent III's De Miseria Humanae Conditionis. It belongs to the devotional-contemplative strand of his output, alongside De Operatione Divini Amoris and De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum, and it rehearses the familiar themes — death, judgement, the emptiness of honours and riches — in the sober monastic register of his shorter treatises.

Mainz, 1495 · Latin / English

Ecloga de Laude Calvorum ad Carolum (Hucbald of Elnon, transmitted by Trithemius)

An Eclogue in Praise of Bald Men, to Charles (Hucbald of Elnon; in Trithemius’s transcription) · 1496first English

The Ecloga de Laude Calvorum ad Carolum — "An Eclogue in Praise of Bald Men, to Charles" — is one of the legendary curiosities of medieval Latin literature: a 133-line poem in which every single word begins with the letter C. It is a lipogrammatic tour de force, an entire mock-encomium conducted under that one constraint — the bald-headed are like the sun, like the moon, like polished bronze, like a clear and unclouded sky — and the constraint is the joke as much as the praise. Composed in the Carolingian ninth century and addressed to the emperor Charles the Bald, it earned its author a small immortality outside his more serious musical and hagiographic writings.

Mainz, 1496 · Latin / English

De Cura Pastorali

On Pastoral Care · 1496first English

De Cura Pastorali — "On Pastoral Care" — is Trithemius's treatise on the duties of those charged with the care of souls, in the long tradition of clerical-formation literature descending from Gregory the Great's Regula Pastoralis. It sits among his writings on the priestly and clerical life — alongside Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis and De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda — rather than his strictly monastic-reform tracts, though the two strands overlap in his work. Its concern is the rector's responsibility for those under his cure: preaching, correction, the example of life, and the burden of office.

Mainz [not before 1496, 1496 · Latin / English

De Purissima et Immaculata Conceptione Virginis (Buda)

On the Most Pure and Immaculate Conception of the Virgin (Buda edition) · 1497first English

De Purissima et Immaculata Conceptione Virginis — "On the Most Pure and Immaculate Conception of the Virgin" — is Trithemius's defence of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary, then a contested theological question rather than defined dogma, with Dominicans and Franciscans sharply divided. Trithemius argues for the Franciscan, pro-Immaculist side in the scholastic manner, and the work is continuous with his St Anne and Marian writings — the devotional-hagiographic strand of his early Sponheim output carried into doctrinal polemic.

2 editions: Nürnberg, 1497 · Argentoratum, 1506

De Operatione Divini Amoris

On the Working of Divine Love · 1497first English

De Operatione Divini Amoris — "On the Working of Divine Love" — is one of Trithemius's devotional-contemplative works, treating the action of divine love in the soul. It belongs with the inward, affective side of his output rather than the polemical reform tracts or the cryptographic books, and stands near his other contemplative pieces in the corpus — De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum and De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae. Where the reform writings address the discipline of the cloister, this one turns to the inner motion of charity that the discipline is meant to serve.

Mainz, 1497 · Latin / English

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum

On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks · 1498first English

Liber de Triplici Regione Claustralium et Spirituali Exercitio Monachorum — "On the Threefold Region of Cloister-dwellers and the Spiritual Exercise of Monks" — is Trithemius's ascetic guide to the monastic life, mapping the monk's progress through three "regions" or stages of interior discipline: purification for beginners, illumination for the proficient, and union with God for the perfect — a scheme drawn from Pseudo-Dionysius and the Victorines and adapted to Benedictine observance. He completed it in manuscript in 1497; it is one of the central texts of his Sponheim reform programme, alongside the Sermones ad Monachos and De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis.

1500s

De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum

On the True Conversion of the Mind to God · 1500first English

De Vera Conversione Mentis ad Deum — "On the True Conversion of the Mind to God" — is one of Trithemius's devotional-contemplative treatises, on the soul's genuine turning toward God as opposed to a merely outward religious life. It sits with the inward, affective side of his work — De Operatione Divini Amoris, De Vanitate et Miseria Humanae Vitae — rather than the reform tracts or the cryptographic books, and it treats conversion as an interior act of the will and intellect rather than a change of habit or observance.

Mainz, 1500 · Latin / English

1510s

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem

A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian · 1515first English

Liber Octo Quaestionum ad Maximilianum Caesarem — "A Book of Eight Questions to Emperor Maximilian" — is Trithemius's reply to the eight questions Maximilian put to him at Boppard: on faith and understanding, on the faith necessary for salvation, on the miracles of unbelievers, on witches and harmful magic, and on related matters. Composed in 1508, it is his central statement on witchcraft and the source from which later demonological writers drew heavily. The questions are set out in an enumerated table and answered in sequence, in the blend of scholastic authority and pastoral caution that marks his shorter treatises.

Compendium sive Breviarium primi voluminis Annalium sive Historiarum de origine regum et gentis Francorum

A Compendium or Breviary of the First Volume of the Annals or Histories, on the Origin of the Kings and People of the Franks · 1515first English

Compendium sive Breviarium primi voluminis Annalium sive Historiarum de origine regum et gentis Francorum — "A Compendium of the First Volume of the Annals on the Origin of the Kings and People of the Franks" — is Trithemius's condensed history of Frankish origins, dedicated to Lorenz von Bibra, Bishop of Würzburg. It is an abridgment of the larger annalistic project of his Würzburg years, and it shares the legendary-genealogical method characteristic of his historiography: a Trojan / Sicambrian descent for the Franks that later scholarship has treated with considerable caution. The compendium form makes it the most readable entry point into his Frankish history, set out year by year from the origins to the Carolingians.

Mainz, 1515 · Latin / English

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos

Sermons and Exhortations to Monks · 1516first English

Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Sermons and Exhortations to Monks" — collects Trithemius's addresses to the monastic community at Sponheim during his reforming abbacy (1483–1506). The sermons are practical spiritual direction for Benedictine monks: on obedience, humility, the discipline of the choir, the dangers of private property, and the interior life that the Rule is meant to form. They sit at the heart of the monastic-reform cluster, alongside De Statu et Ruina Monastici Ordinis and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — less a systematic treatise than the abbot's own voice, pressing his monks toward the observance he wanted for them.

2 editions: Argentine, 1516 · Argentine, 1516

Clavis Polygraphiae

Key to the Polygraphia · 1518

Clavis Polygraphiae — the "Key to the Polygraphia" — is Trithemius's own commentary on his Polygraphiae libri sex, explaining how the six books of cipher tables are constructed and how a correspondent is meant to use them in practice. A cipher manual is of little use without its key, and the Clavis is what made the Polygraphiae operational: it walks through the modi of enciphering and deciphering, the Ave Maria alphabets, and the polyalphabetic tables, tying the abstract apparatus of the six books to the concrete business of sending and recovering a hidden message. It was composed alongside the Polygraphiae in 1508 and printed with it.

Basel, 1518 · Latin / English

Polygraphiae libri VI (Basel: Furter & Petri, for Haselberg, 1518)

Six Books of Polygraphy (Basel, 1518 first edition) · 1518

Polygraphiae libri VI — "Six Books of Polygraphy" — is the 1518 first edition of Trithemius's open cryptographic manual, the first printed book on cryptography in the West. He completed the work late in life — the dedication to Emperor Maximilian I is dated 1508 — and it was printed posthumously, two years after his death. Where the Steganographia hides its ciphers behind angel-magic, the Polygraphiae teaches the craft in the open: substitution tables, transposition grids, the "Ave Maria" cipher in which any plaintext becomes a pious Latin sentence, and numerical codes. Its six books move from simple to complex, culminating in the polyalphabetic tabula recta.

1520s

De Septem Secundeis, id est, Intelligentiis sive Spiritibus Orbes post Deum Moventibus

On the Seven Secondary Intelligences, that is, the Spirits Moving the Orbs after God · 1522

De Septem Secundeis, id est, Intelligentiis sive Spiritibus Orbes post Deum Moventibus — "On the Seven Secondary Intelligences, that is, the Spirits Moving the Orbs after God" — is Trithemius's astrological philosophy of history. Its thesis is that the successive ages of the world are governed in turn by seven planetary angels — the secundeis — each ruling for a fixed period in the order of the celestial spheres, yielding a chronological scheme that runs from the Creation down to his own century. Addressed to Emperor Maximilian I, it is the work in which Trithemius brought his reading of the celestial-intelligence tradition (transmitted through Arabic and scholastic astronomy) to bear on universal history, and it had an outsized afterlife in Renaissance historical thought.

De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda Libellus

A Little Book on Establishing the Life of Priests · 1577first English

De Sacerdotum Vita Instituenda Libellus — "A Little Book on Establishing the Life of Priests" — is Trithemius's short treatise on ordering the life and conduct of priests, close in subject to his Institutio Vitae Sacerdotalis and De Cura Pastorali. It belongs to the clerical-formation side of his work rather than the strictly monastic reform tracts: the "little book" of the title signals a compact, practical manual — how a priest is to be formed in virtue and learning — rather than a sustained treatise.

1600s

Opera Historica, Part I

Collected Historical Works (Freher ed.), first part · 1601first English

Opera Historica — "Historical Works," Part I — is the collected historical magnum opus of Trithemius's last years, assembling his chronicle of the Franks from their mythical Trojan origins through the Merovingian and Carolingian dynasties to the late medieval period. It follows the universal-chronicle tradition — year-by-year entries assembled from over two hundred manuscript sources — and is an important, if at times credulous, source for early medieval history. (Part II, the Hirsau and Sponheim monastic chronicles, is prdl-70290 in this corpus.) Like much of Trithemius's historical writing it mingles genuine documentary labour with fabricated sources, the most notorious being the invented Hunibald; readers should weigh it against later scholarship, but the breadth of compilation is real.

Francofurti, 1601 · Latin / English

Opera Historica, Part II — Chronicon Hirsaugiense & Sponheimense

Collected Historical Works, second part: the Hirsau and Sponheim chronicles · 1601first English

Opera Historica, Part II — the Chronicon Hirsaugiense and Chronicon Sponheimense — is the second half of Trithemius's collected historical works: his two great monastic chronicles. The Chronicon Hirsaugiense narrates the foundation and progress of the monastery of Hirsau, in the diocese of Speyer, down to 1520; the Chronicon Sponheimense does the same for his own former house of Sponheim, in the diocese of Mainz. Together they are the fullest record of the Benedictine reform world he inhabited — though, like his Frankish history, they must be read with caution for the fabricated sources woven into the genuine documentary labour.

Francofurti, 1601 · Latin / English

Clavis Generalis Triplex in Libros Steganographicos

Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books · 1608

Clavis Generalis Triplex in Libros Steganographicos — the "Threefold General Key to the Steganographic Books" — is Trithemius's own explanatory key to his most notorious work, the Steganographia. The Steganographia (composed around 1499–1500) circulated only in manuscript during his lifetime and earned him lasting accusations of necromancy, because its cipher instructions are dressed as conjurations of angels and spirits; it was printed posthumously in 1606 and placed on the Index. The Clavis is the antidote Trithemius supplied: a compact decryption key demonstrating that the "spirit names" resolve into a cryptographic system, not a magical one. It sets out, modus by modus, the explicit substitution alphabets by which each cipher is to be read.

Veterum Sophorum Sigilla et Imagines Magicae (pseudo-Trithemian, 1612)

Seals and Magical Images of the Ancient Sages (pseudo-Trithemian astral-magic text) · 1612first English

Veterum Sophorum Sigilla et Imagines Magicae — "The Seals and Magical Images of the Ancient Sages" — is a short astral-magical text: instructions for engraving planetary seals and images on stones and gems, keyed to the divine name Tetragrammaton and the courses of the planets, "for producing miraculous effects." It belongs to the later esoteric corpus that attached itself to Trithemius's name after his death.

Trithemius Sui Ipsius Vindex

Trithemius, Vindicator of Himself · 1616first English

Trithemius Sui Ipsius Vindex — "Trithemius, Vindicator of Himself" — is the abbot's apologetic answer to the accusations of demonic magic that dogged his last decade. His Steganographia, circulated in manuscript from the late 1490s and reaching readers it was not meant to reach — Carolus Bovillus among them — had been read at face value as a manual of necromancy, and the charge clung to him; the Vindex, printed posthumously in 1616, gathers his own protestations of orthodoxy alongside the testimony of allies, insisting that the Steganographia is cryptography dressed as conjuration, not magic at all. It is the apologetic counterpart to the Steganographia (prdl-24395) and the Clavis Generalis Triplex (prdl-70281) elsewhere in this corpus.

1620s

Steganographia, hoc est: Ars per occultam scripturam

Steganography: The Art of Hidden Writing · 1621

The Steganographia is Trithemius's most famous and most notorious work: a treatise in three books, written about 1499–1500 and circulated for a century in manuscript before it was first printed (Frankfurt, 1606). On its surface it is a manual of angel-magic — long conjurations addressed to spirit-princes and their subordinate spirits, each governing a quarter of the heavens, a wind, or an hour of the day. Beneath that surface it is a cryptographic system: the "conjurations" are cover-text, and the real message is carried by the spirit-names and the numeric keys tabulated for each prince. It was the disguise that undid him. Manuscript copies reached readers they were not meant for — Carolus Bovillus among them — who took the spirit-magic at face value and accused Trithemius of necromancy; the book was placed on the Index, and the third book's reputation as genuinely demonic persisted until its cipher was solved — first by Thomas Ernst (1996), then independently by Jim Reeds (1998). Trithemius's own answer to the charge is the Trithemius sui ipsius vindex of 1616, also in this corpus (prdl-32287).

Darmbstadii. Ex officina typographica Balthasaris Aulæandri, 1621 · Latin / English

Admonitiones / Exhortationes ad Monachos

Admonitions and Exhortations to Monks (later collected reprint) · original date uncertainfirst English

Admonitiones / Exhortationes ad Monachos — "Admonitions and Exhortations to Monks" — gathers Trithemius's monastic-reform addresses: calls to stricter observance of the Benedictine Rule, to the interior life of the cloister, and to the duties of the professed monk. They belong to the reforming side of his abbacy — of a piece with the Sermones et Exhortationes ad Monachos and De Triplici Regione Claustralium — and they show the abbot as pastor rather than polymath, urging his monks toward the discipline that his historical and cryptographic works were sometimes thought to have distracted him from.
